procedural_history.originating_court: Second Additional Sessions Judge, Ambikapur (Trial Court)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order by the Trial Court which the High Court deemed not to be a judgment.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Full Court of the High Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur, on its administrative side, concluded that the Trial Court had not passed a valid judgment. Consequently, the High Court treated the trial as pending and transferred the case from the Court of Second Additional Sessions Judge, Ambikapur, to the Court of District and Sessions Judge, Surguja at Ambikapur for rehearing and disposal. This decision was communicated to the Sessions Judge by the Registrar General of the High Court. This order was challenged in Writ Appeal Nos. 174 of 2016 and 181 of 2016, which were both dismissed by the High Court in a Judgment and Order dated 24.08.2016.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court, arguing that the Trial Court's order *was* a judgment, and that the High Court could not administratively order a rehearing. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals.

directions: The trial court to whom the cases have been transferred is directed to proceed in accordance with law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the trial judge's declaration of the result of acquittal, without a written, signed, and dated judgment being available on record, constitutes a valid pronouncement of judgment under the CrPC.

facts: A trial judge, after the conclusion of a criminal trial, recorded in the order sheet that the accused persons had been acquitted.
However, the judgment was not dictated or pronounced in open court.
An inquiry later found that no complete judgment was available on record.
An incomplete, unsigned, 14-page typed draft was found, but it was not a finished or signed judgment.
law: The Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), under Section 353, mandates that a judgment must be pronounced in open court.
This can be done by delivering the whole judgment, reading out the whole judgment, or reading out the operative part and explaining its substance.
A document cannot be considered a valid judgment unless it is complete, signed, and dated by the presiding officer.
application: The Court determined that the trial judge failed to follow the mandatory procedures for pronouncing a judgment as laid out in the CrPC.
It distinguished between merely announcing the 'result' of a case and the formal 'pronouncement' of a judgment.
The Court reasoned that the non-availability of a complete, signed judgment meant that, legally, no judgment existed.
The incomplete and unsigned draft found on record did not meet the legal requirements of a judgment under Section 353 CrPC.
The Court described the act of declaring a result without an actual judgment in existence as a 'gross illegality'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the trial judge's declaration of acquittal was not a valid judgment. Because no complete, signed, and dated judgment was pronounced in open court as required by the CrPC, the Court concluded that no judgment had been delivered and the trial was still pending.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in the exercise of its administrative and supervisory powers under Article 227 of the Constitution, was competent to treat the trial as pending and transfer the case to another court for rehearing, upon finding that no valid judgment had been pronounced by the trial judge.

facts: A trial court judge recorded in the case's order sheet that the accused had been acquitted, stating the judgment was separately typed, signed, and dated.
Following a complaint, an inquiry by the High Court revealed that no such judgment was actually available on record because it had never been dictated, dated, or signed by the judge.
The Full Court of the High Court, acting on its administrative side, concluded that no valid judgment had been passed.
Consequently, the High Court treated the trial as still pending and transferred the case to a different court for a complete rehearing and disposal.
law: Article 227 of the Constitution of India confers broad powers of superintendence on the High Court over all subordinate courts and tribunals within its jurisdiction.
This power is not confined to administrative matters but also includes judicial review to ensure lower courts act within their authority.
The High Court can exercise this power of superintendence *suo motu* (on its own initiative) to address administrative exigencies and expediencies.
application: The Supreme Court found that since the trial judge had never actually dictated, signed, or pronounced a judgment, the entry in the order sheet about an acquittal had no legal effect. Therefore, the trial was never legally concluded and was still pending.
The Court reasoned that the High Court was under a "legal obligation" to rectify this "grave error" to further the cause of justice.

The High Court's power of superintendence under Article 227 was deemed broad enough to cover this situation. The decision to treat the case as pending and transfer it was a valid exercise of its administrative and supervisory authority.

The Court rejected the argument that such a transfer could only be made on the judicial side (under Section 407 CrPC), affirming that the High Court's administrative powers were sufficient to address this unique procedural failure.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court acted competently and found "no illegality" in its decision. It held that under its administrative and supervisory powers granted by Article 227, the High Court was justified in treating the trial as pending and transferring it to another court for rehearing, as no valid judgment had ever been pronounced.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the trial judge's declaration of the result of acquittal, without a written, signed, and dated judgment being available on record, constitutes a valid pronouncement of judgment under the CrPC.
appellant_arguments: The trial judge's entry in the order sheet, stating that the accused were acquitted as per a separately typed, signed, and dated judgment, should be considered a valid pronouncement.
An incomplete typed judgment of 14 pages was found on record, which indicates that a judgment did exist.
respondent_arguments: The approach of the High Court, which found no valid judgment was passed, is correct.
A valid judgment requires pronouncement in open court; simply announcing the result is insufficient.
The judgment was not dictated in open court, and a complete, signed, and dated judgment was not available on record, which is a prerequisite for a valid judgment.
Non-availability of a judgment on record means no judgment was ever delivered.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in the exercise of its administrative and supervisory powers under Article 227 of the Constitution, was competent to treat the trial as pending and transfer the case to another court for rehearing, upon finding that no valid judgment had been pronounced by the trial judge.
appellant_arguments: The High Court cannot transfer a case in the exercise of its administrative authority.
The power to transfer a case can only be exercised on the judicial side under Section 407 of the CrPC.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's approach was 'absolutely infallible' and does not warrant interference.

Since the High Court correctly found that no valid judgment had been passed, it was competent to resolve on the administrative side that the matter should be reheard by another judge to complete the pending trial.

cases.principle: Under Article 227, every High Court has the power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals within its jurisdiction, which entitles it to pass orders for administrative exigency and expediency and to exercise this power suo motu.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A High Court is under a legal obligation to set aside an order from a lower court that is a mere declaration of a result without a judgment, as such an order has no effect in law and must be nullified.
obiter: The practice of High Courts announcing the result of a case with 'reasons to follow' is undesirable, as their orders are subject to appellate jurisdiction, unlike the final orders of the Supreme Court.
The inherent power of a court cannot be exercised to do that which is specifically prohibited by the Code of Criminal Procedure, such as altering or reviewing a final judgment.
Every High Court has the power of superintendence over all subordinate courts and tribunals within its jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A mere declaration of the result of a case, such as an acquittal, without a written, signed, and dated judgment being pronounced in open court and made available on the record, does not constitute a valid judgment under the CrPC. In such a situation of a procedural void, the High Court is empowered under its administrative and supervisory jurisdiction of Article 227 of the Constitution to rectify the grave error by treating the trial as pending and transferring it for a rehearing to ensure the cause of justice is served.
legal_tests_applied: A valid judgment requires it to be an expression of an opinion after due consideration of the facts, which is pronounced in open court, signed, and dated. The reading of the operative part is permissible, but this presupposes the existence of a complete judgment.

The power of superintendence under Article 227 of the Constitution entitles the High Court to pass orders for administrative exigency and expediency to rectify grave errors and ensure the sanctity of justice is not undermined.
The prohibition in Section 362 CrPC against a court altering or reviewing its judgment does not apply where no valid judgment was ever pronounced in the first place.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the trial judge's order amounted to a judgment was rejected because a valid judgment requires more than just an announcement of the result. The court found that the "Non- availability of judgment, can never be a judgment because there is no declaration by way of pronouncement in the open court that the accused has been convicted or acquitted."

The appellant's contention that the High Court could only transfer a case on its judicial side under Section 407 CrPC was incorrect. The court held that since no valid judgment had been passed, the High Court was competent to act under its administrative and supervisory powers, stating, "Under Article 227 of the Constitution of India every High Court has superintendence over all courts and tribunals... and it is trite that this power of superintendence entitles the High Court to pass orders for administrative exigency and expediency."
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position that no valid judgment was ever delivered was affirmed. The court reasoned that, "Without pronouncement of a judgment in the open court, signed and dated, it is difficult to treat it as a judgment of conviction."

The respondent's argument that the High Court acted correctly was upheld. The court found that the High Court had a "duty to see that sanctity of justice is not undermined" and that by "rectifying the grave error has acted in furtherance of the cause of. justice."

The court agreed that because no valid judgment existed, the High Court was correct to treat the trial as pending and, in the exercise of its administrative power, transfer the case for rehearing and disposal.
policy_considerations: "Performance of judicial duty in the manner prescribed by law is fundamental to the concept of rule of law in a democratic State."
"The plinth of justice dispensation system is founded on the faith, trust and confidence of the people and nothing can be allowed to contaminate and corrode the same."
"A litigant who comes to a court of law expects that inherent and essential principles of adjudication... shall be followed and ultimately there shall be a reasoned verdict."
"The result of such trial is to end in a judgment as required to be pronounced in accordance with law. And, that is how the stability of the creditability in the institution is maintained."

The court highlighted the "serious difficulties" that arise from the practice of pronouncing a final order without a reasoned judgment, as it places the appellate court in a "predicament" and often leads to the stay of such orders, defeating the purpose of speedy justice.
